justice: Most spatial resources are devoted to multiple wide motor-vehicle lanes, while the pedestrian realm is limited to narrow edge sidewalks and no visible dedicated bicycle lane.
The sidewalks on both sides appear continuous, but there are no clearly visible curb ramps, tactile paving, or pedestrian crossing facilities at this large intersection.
Signal heads and lane markings prioritize through traffic efficiency for drivers more than equal accommodation of walking and cycling users.
safety: The road is very wide with several high-speed travel lanes, which can increase crash severity and make crossings difficult for non-motorized users.
Traffic signals, streetlights, and clear lane markings improve driver guidance and reduce some operational conflict.
There is no visible protected bike lane, marked crosswalk, or pedestrian refuge island, leaving cyclists and pedestrians exposed at the intersection edge.
livability: The corridor is lined mainly by roadway, landscaping strips, and open land, with very limited visible shops, services, or active building frontage.
The broad sidewalks and planted edges offer some spatial openness, but the street lacks visible benches, bus stops, or social gathering amenities.
Low visible pedestrian presence and sparse street-side activity suggest weak everyday street life and limited community interaction.
sustainability: Rows of street trees and planted medians provide green infrastructure and some ecological value along the corridor.
The very wide carriageway encourages automobile-oriented movement and consumes substantial paved surface area.
No visible dedicated cycling facilities or obvious public transit infrastructure reduce support for lower-carbon travel choices.
aesthetics: The avenue has a clean, orderly appearance with consistent lane markings, aligned light poles, and a symmetrical roadside tree layout.
Landscaped medians, flower beds, and tree rows add visual structure and soften the large roadway.
The oversized asphalt surface and sparse urban frontage make the scene feel somewhat monotonous despite the neat maintenance.
comfort: Young street trees are present, but canopy cover is still limited, so thermal comfort appears weak under strong sun exposure.
The sidewalks look relatively smooth and unobstructed, which supports basic physical walking comfort.
There are no visible benches, shelters, or shaded waiting areas, reducing resting comfort for people spending time on foot.
The low traffic volume at the moment may reduce noise stress, but the large road width can still feel psychologically exposed for pedestrians and cyclists.
walkability: Sidewalks are present and appear paved continuously along both sides of the road.
The intersection environment is scaled for vehicles, with a very long crossing distance and no visible zebra crossing or pedestrian signal features in view.
Sparse shade, minimal active frontage, and lack of visible pedestrian amenities make walking less attractive for everyday trips.
bikeability: There is no visible dedicated or protected bicycle lane on this corridor.
The wide, fast-moving motor-vehicle lanes and large intersection geometry create an intimidating environment for on-road cycling.
No visible bicycle parking, bike markings, or cycle-specific signals are provided to support convenient and safe cycling.
